title: Coming of age
hook: the pen is lifted from the child, until one day it isn't

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first khatm, and your line: a child finishes. Did you tell a young learner you noticed the work? Today the child grows up, and something quietly changes. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

For years a child prays beside a parent, copies the bows, maybe tries a half-day fast in Ramadan to see what it's like. All of it is real, and all of it is welcome. And yet, in Islamic teaching, there's a line waiting up ahead. One day, with no ceremony required, the child crosses it. A hadith describes the time before that line with a striking picture: the pen is lifted. Today: the day the pen comes down, and the word for what begins.
screen: `PRAYING BESIDE A PARENT.` → `A LINE WAITING UP AHEAD.` → `THE PEN IS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in Sunan Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase: the pen is lifted from three. From the sleeper until he wakes. From the child until he reaches maturity. And from the one who has lost his reason until he recovers it. Commentators read the pen as the one that records a person's deeds against them. Before maturity, nothing is yet written against a child. That's the first thing: childhood is protected time. But protected isn't empty. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, a woman on the pilgrimage lifts up a small child and asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: does he have a Hajj? He answers: yes, and you have a reward. The child's good deeds are welcomed. Second, the word. Taklif means being given a charge, a responsibility. A person who has reached it is called mukallaf: one who is now responsible. Scholars set out the signs of maturity, and the schools differ on the details, but the idea is shared: at maturity, the duties begin. Prayer, fasting, the rest. Now it counts. Third, the charge comes with a limit. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." In Arabic, that verse's verb is yukallifu, from the same root as taklif. The charge and its limit, in one sentence. Fourth, look at what this does to the years before. The khatm, the prayers beside a parent, the half fasts: none of it was required. It was practice, freely given. Taklif doesn't erase that. It builds on it. The child who already knows the movements walks into responsibility already holding them.
screen: `THE PEN IS LIFTED FROM THREE.` · `TAKLIF: GIVEN A CHARGE.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · `PRACTICE BECOMES RESPONSIBILITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about responsibility. Settle, and breathe. Recall a moment when something in your life started to count: a first job, a key of your own, a promise that was yours to keep. What changed, and what stayed the same? Then name one responsibility you carry now that fits you, not one beyond your scope. And let this part of the path pass by: the call in the ear, the date, the name, the 'aqiqah, the hair, khitan, prayer at seven, the khatm, and now taklif. A whole childhood. The bell holds the time.
Taklif. Being given a charge: at maturity, the duties of the faith begin, and none beyond a soul's scope. Today's word.
Your line: now it counts. Today, take one thing you're responsible for and give it your full attention. Tomorrow, a new part of the path: choosing a spouse. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In Islamic law, a person becomes mukallaf at maturity, and from then on prayer, fasting and the other duties are required of them; before that, children are encouraged to practice and their good deeds are welcomed.

original.note: Arabic: a charge laid on someone; religious responsibility.

trapdoor: what you thought: the birthday when you become an adult.
what it means: the point of maturity when prayer, fasting and the other duties begin: now it counts.
what a scholar hears: the pen lifted from three (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi), the person becoming mukallaf, and 2:286, where the verb yukallifu sets the limit of every charge.
